sm: The hosts, including Jared Longshore, Nate Wilson, Doug Wilson and Joe Rigney, open the second week of No Quarter November and turn to the midterm elections held a week earlier. They note that the Senate re-elected John Thune as majority leader despite Republicans losing nine seats. Doug argues the swing was mainly a middle finger from an angry, uninformed electorate rather than a principled shift, and that Democrats talk openly of aggressive prosecutions of Trump's family and staffers. The group says many swing voters act on opinions and moods, not convictions, and notes young men swung sharply from Trump in 2024 to the other side this time.

The discussion continues on the young male swing, with the view that the populace is manic depressive and that Democrats achieved presidential-level turnout in a midterm because Trump drives liberal turnout. Doug points out that millions of new voters come out of government schools each year, so polling of young people involves different people over time. Speakers compare the shift to fair-weather sports fans jumping on a winning team. They say the Iran war hurt Trump's momentum mainly through bad messaging, such as repeated claims it would last only three weeks, and through an orchestrated social media campaign. They compare it to how the Tet offensive was spun as a defeat.

The hosts say the left channeled anger toward Israel and Netanyahu and pushed the idea that Trump is a puppet, giving swing voters someone else to blame. They describe the whole thing as a mojo contest, comparing the Venezuela success with the Iran war, and say the internet makes mood swings faster but human nature is unchanged. Doug thinks the right deserved some of the loss and that this gives Republicans a better chance in 2028. He expects the likely candidates to be Vance, Rubio, Cruz and DeSantis, with some distancing from Israel but no break with MAGA. They also note that anti-trans measures passed easily on state ballots.

The group notes that voters backed such ballot measures yet re-elected politicians who opposed them, including Arizona's Democratic governor, calling the public incoherent. They contrast Florida under DeSantis, who they call competent, conservative and willing to pick culture war fights that repel unwanted people, with Texas under Abbott and Idaho's governor, who they describe as weaker Republicans. They discuss the Paxton race and the risk of Idaho turning purple. They also discuss the Muslim candidate who won in Michigan with huge margins in Dearborn, concluding that many voters act on tribal, ethnic or religious solidarity rather than ideology.

The hosts tell of a young activist questioning an Egyptian voter in Michigan about transgender issues and say vibes and tribal identity override policy. They argue Americans usually elect the president they would rather have at a barbecue, and tie Dearborn's history to the anti-Semitism of the Henry Ford family. Looking ahead, they predict two years of gridlock, with Trump governing by executive action and the courts, and Democrats having to show what they would do. They also discuss progressive seminarians in the Senate, saying the religious left has always been Christian nationalist, and welcome the state-level conservative measures that passed.

The hosts discuss the religious left, saying liberal Christianity is lame and that Texas Democrat candidate Terrico looks like a soft evangelical pastor. They suggest the future religious left may be Muslim, and add that conservative Christians do better in opposition, on defense. They turn to Latah County in Idaho, where a recount is in progress, the county went redder, and there are now three Republican county commissioners for the first time in fifty years. Doug says the city of Moscow stays far harder to change, which is why they are in several lawsuits with the city. They compare the gains to moving the chains for a first down.

The hosts say Christ Church is growing and newcomers to the county tend to be conservative, though they are far from a foothold able to hold Idaho. Asked how to win a vibes-driven politics, they point to the block party, the Fourth of July parade, school athletics, the Logos campus and renovating an eyesore building, arguing that building beautiful things and changing culture is more compelling than any platform. They recall that Moscow was very different thirty years ago and say Christ Church women average four children, a birth rate comparable to Zambia, Uganda and Togo. They say conservatives are drifting from eat-your-spinach budget politics.

The hosts argue that today's thirteen and fourteen year olds will soon vote locally, and that progressives are aging with about 1.2 children, which they call a strong demographic argument. They say a covenant community makes large families feasible and lets them invest in buildings for generations rather than quick returns, unlike storage units built for maximum return. They celebrate the defeat of Prop One, the abortion measure, in Idaho by about twelve points, with many people knocking on doors. They worry it was smaller than the margin for English as Idaho's language, warn Idaho could become like Texas, and joke about a campaign to wipe the blue off newcomers' shoes.
